tasks.title: Harden open_in_studio's editor token to session-scoped/short-lived
tasks.notes: Deliberate, explicitly tracked simplification from P2-1, not an oversight: open_in_studio currently reuses the single standing EDITOR_API_TOKEN both for the MCP's server-to-server call to Course Studio's POST /api/import AND as the literal ?token= query param in the human-facing editor_url it returns -- i.e. the exact same posture Course Studio's own deep-link mechanism already uses today (editor.js reads ?token= from its own URL on load, see P0-1), so this is not a new weakness, but it is a real one: that URL can end up in chat transcripts, logs, browser history, or get shared/forwarded, and anyone holding it has the SAME standing credential that gates every /api/* route for every session, not just this one. A more defensible design would mint a short-lived and/or single-use, session-scoped credential (e.g. a signed token bound to the specific session id with a short TTL, checked in _require_auth alongside or instead of the standing EDITOR_API_TOKEN) so a leaked deep link only exposes one session for a limited window rather than the whole editor. Real work: extend apps/scorm_editor/server.py's auth model (_require_auth, _read_secret usage) to accept such a scoped token in addition to the standing one (backward compatible), and have open_in_studio mint one instead of reading EDITOR_API_TOKEN into the URL. Out of scope for P2-1 by explicit instruction; not implemented, only recorded here so it isn't silently forgotten. IMPLEMENTED: import_package() (apps/scorm_editor/server.py) now mints secrets.token_urlsafe(24) as open_token, stores only its SHA-256 hash plus an expiry (now + EDITOR_OPEN_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS, default 14400s/4h, new env var) in .editor-meta.json, and returns the plaintext once in import_package's own return dict -- the only place it is ever exposed in plaintext, flowing through POST /api/import's JSON response. New _route_session_id(route) helper is an explicit allowlist of the route shapes carrying a session id as their first segment (/api/course/<sid>, /course/<sid>/<path>, /api/media/<sid>, /api/export/<sid>, /api/revisions/<sid>..., /api/compare/<sid>/..., /api/collaboration/<sid>, /api/sources/<sid>, /api/accessibility/<sid>, /api/localization/<sid>, /api/generation/<sid>); everything else (notably /api/new, /api/import, static shell) returns None so a scoped token can never authenticate those routes, only the standing EDITOR_API_TOKEN can. _require_auth now checks the standing token first (unchanged) and, only on failure, falls through to a new _check_open_token(sid, token) helper that reads .editor-meta.json directly (no _workspace()/_meta() idle-TTL side effects), hashes the presented token, and hmac.compare_digest()s it against the stored hash while checking open_token_expires_at. open_in_studio (src/course_mcp_server/tools.py) now reads imported.get('open_token') and uses it for the deep link instead of the standing EDITOR_API_TOKEN; if absent (older Course Studio), falls back to the standing token and records that fallback via _record() rather than silently reusing the broader credential.

tasks.title: Studio save-back: pull Course-Studio-edited content into the MCP project model
tasks.notes:
Investigated fresh before dispatch and found a real, non-obvious data-loss bug in the 'obvious' naive design before any worker touched code: _project_course_payload (the function every content-reading tool, including build_export_package/validate_superior_course_quality, calls to get 'the current authoritative course content') pipes the course_content artifact through _course_payload_from_submission EVERY TIME IT'S READ, not once at write time -- and that transform RECOMPUTES each lesson's objective field from objective_ids + learning_objectives on every call, discarding whatever is actually present in the input's own objective field. Course Studio's course.json is ALREADY in the post-transform, player-facing shape (confirmed: apps/scorm_editor/server.py's create_course() builds a fresh course via the same exporter, so Studio's shape matches the exporter's OUTPUT, not the pre-transform agent-authoring INPUT). Naively storing Studio-edited course.json as a new course_content artifact would mean any human who directly edits a lesson's objective text in Course Studio -- a completely normal, expected edit -- would have that edit SILENTLY DISCARDED on the very next read, replaced by a stale recomputed value. This is real, silent data loss in exactly the core use case this feature exists for, and it would not have been caught by a naive 'does the artifact get stored' test.

FIX specified precisely in the brief and implemented: a new, distinct artifact type, studio_content, stored as-is (no transform, since it's already correctly shaped). _project_course_payload checks studio_content FIRST and short-circuits to return it directly when present, only falling through to the existing course_content/legacy logic otherwise -- making a Studio edit genuinely and permanently authoritative on every subsequent read, while leaving the existing agent-authored path completely untouched for projects that never touch Course Studio. The artifact TYPE itself (studio_content vs. course_content) doubles as the provenance signal distinguishing human-edited from agent-authored content -- confirmed provenance.py is a different concern entirely (cryptographic export-signing, not authorship tracking) and correctly left untouched rather than extended for a purpose it doesn't serve.

New tool import_studio_edits(project_id, session_id): pulls GET /api/course/<session_id> from Course Studio using the same EDITOR_API_TOKEN/EDITOR_INTERNAL_URL/urllib pattern open_in_studio already established, does a deliberately permissive structural sanity check (dict + modules list + lessons list, nothing stricter) rather than full CourseProjectV2 schema validation -- confirmed correct reasoning: that stricter schema is the pre-transform agent-authoring contract, and holding a human's ad-hoc Studio edit to it would reject perfectly normal edits. Session id is supplied by the caller (the agent already has it from open_in_studio's own earlier response) rather than persisted MCP-side, since nothing on the project currently remembers which Studio session it was opened into and adding that persistence wasn't necessary for this task.
evidence: Worker's own tests: 7 new in tests/test_import_studio_edits.py -- success, Course Studio unreachable, session not found (HTTPError), malformed course, not-configured, and the SPECIFIC regression test proving the diagnosed bug is fixed: a lesson's objective_ids/learning_objectives deliberately left untouched while only the objective TEXT is edited, pulled via import_studio_edits, and confirmed to survive a fresh _project_course_payload read afterward

tasks.title: Wire HeyGenPresenterProvider into real MCP tools (submit + poll-again shape)
tasks.notes:
BEFORE writing the worker brief, investigating the actual persistence question surfaced a critical, load-bearing bug in the P3-3 adapter that would have broken this entire task: HeyGenPresenterProvider.poll()/.fetch() required the job to already exist in THAT SPECIFIC instance's in-memory self._jobs dict, populated only by a prior submit() call on the SAME instance. Since a real two-tool-call flow (submit in one MCP call, poll in a later, separate call) necessarily constructs a fresh provider instance per call -- confirmed by reading how generate_narration_audio already does exactly this for ElevenLabsNarrationProvider -- every real poll()/fetch() call in this design would have raised 'Unknown HeyGen job id' immediately, 100% of the time, despite the job genuinely existing and progressing on HeyGen's servers. This slipped through P3-3's own tests because every one of them called submit+poll+fetch on the SAME provider instance within a single test function -- never simulating the actual cross-call boundary this task exists to build.

Fixed directly by the orchestrator before dispatch (small, well-understood, immediately testable, not deferred to the worker): poll() now get-or-creates local job state instead of raising on an unseen job_id, and always makes a real HTTP status check using only the plain job_id string -- HeyGen's status endpoint is stateless from the client's perspective and needs nothing else. fetch() now self-heals by calling poll() internally if it doesn't already have a locally-cached 'completed' status, rather than requiring the caller to have already polled on that exact instance. Verified against all 15 existing HeyGen tests (unchanged, all still pass) and added one new test proving the actual guarantee: a completely fresh provider instance, given only a job_id string and zero shared state, can genuinely poll and fetch a job submitted by a different instance.

With that fixed, designed the two-tool flow: generate_presenter_video (submits via HeyGenPresenterProvider().submit(), does not block, records a 'presenter_video_job' project artifact via the existing add_artifact/_project_or_raise pattern -- NOT job_store.py, which was confirmed too flat a shape [record_job/get_job_status only carry job_id/status/message, no structured payload] for this state) and check_presenter_video_status (reads the project's latest presenter_video_job artifact for the job_id -- this IS the tenant-isolation boundary, since there is no bare job_id-only lookup surface at all -- polls, and on completion fetches + stores via object_store.store_path + appends a new completed artifact, matching the append-only artifact pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase).

This degrades safely -- a real HeyGenError from an unconfigured/invalid key is still caught by the existing try/except VideoProviderError and returned as a clean 'poll_failed' error, not a crash -- but the error code/message would be less specific than the dedicated 'provider_not_configured' path generate_presenter_video uses.
